say.en: Exporters compete with the whole world. The government refunds some duties, sets up special zones, insures export payments and trains exporters. Let us see how. In this lesson: Explain incentives for foreign trade promotion.
Name organisations that support exporters.
State the objectives and functions of the WTO.

body.en: Incentives: the duty drawback scheme refunds excise and customs duties paid on goods or inputs that are exported; export manufacturing under bond allows production without paying duties; exports are exempt from indirect taxes; the advance authorisation scheme allows duty-free import of inputs used for export production; the EPCG scheme allows import of capital goods at concessional duty against an export obligation; Special Economic Zones (SEZs) and 100% Export Oriented Units (EOUs) offer a duty-free environment; star export houses get special benefits. *Organisational support*: the Department of Commerce, Export Promotion Councils, Commodity Boards, the Export Inspection Council, the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT), the Indian Institute of Packaging (IIP), the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO), ECGC, which insures exporters against non-payment, and EXIM Bank, which finances foreign trade.
body.kn: ಸುಂಕ ಮರುಪಾವತಿ, ಸುಂಕರಹಿತ ಕಚ್ಚಾವಸ್ತು, ವಿಶೇಷ ಆರ್ಥಿಕ ವಲಯಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಇಸಿಜಿಸಿ, ಎಕ್ಸಿಮ್ ಬ್ಯಾಂಕ್‌ನಂತಹ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಗಳ ಮೂಲಕ ಸರ್ಕಾರ ರಫ್ತುದಾರರಿಗೆ ನೆರವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.

body.en: The WTO was established on 1 January 1995 as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT, 1948). Its headquarters is in Geneva, and India is a founder member. Objectives: raise standards of living, ensure full employment, expand production and trade, make optimal use of world resources, protect the environment, and ensure that developing countries get a fair share of *world trade*. Functions: promote an environment in which members negotiate trade agreements, administer those agreements, settle trade disputes between members, review national trade policies, and cooperate with the IMF and the World Bank.

problem.en: An auto-parts exporter near Bengaluru pays ₹2,00,000 as customs duty on imported steel used to make parts that are all exported. Under the duty drawback scheme, 90% of this duty is refunded. How much does the exporter get back, and why does the government do this?

steps.en: Refunding duties lowers the cost of exports so that Indian goods can compete abroad.

answer.en: ₹1,80,000 is refunded; it makes exports more competitive.

narration.en: Let us work through this together. An auto-parts exporter near Bengaluru pays ₹2,00,000 as customs duty on imported steel used to make parts that are all exported. Under the duty drawback scheme, 90% of this duty is refunded. How much does the exporter get back, and why does the government do this?

say.en: Let us work through this together. An auto-parts exporter near Bengaluru pays 2,00,000 rupees as customs duty on imported steel used to make parts that are all exported. Under the duty drawback scheme, 90 percent of this duty is refunded. How much does the exporter get back, and why does the government do this?
Refund equals 90 percent times 2,00,000 rupees equals 1,80,000 rupees.
Net duty borne equals 2,00,000 rupees minus 1,80,000 rupees equals 20,000 rupees.
Refunding duties lowers the cost of exports so that Indian goods can compete abroad.
So the answer is 1,80,000 rupees is refunded; it makes exports more competitive.
